statement: CRS reports that the 2024 estimates of the unauthorized population ranged from 14.6 million to 15.8 million, and that there are no official counts.
anchor: There are no official counts of unauthorized immigrants living in the United States.
In 2024, the unauthorized population was estimated to range between 14.6 million to 15.8 million individuals living in the United States.
context: CRS (nonpartisan), updated 2026-09-22. The range spans the Center for Migration Studies (14.6 million) and the Migration Policy Institute (15.8 million) estimates; CRS does not name them in this passage. Model estimates, not counts. The last full DHS OHSS series found (January 2022) is older; no OHSS estimate for 2024-26 was located.

statement: Pew Research Center estimated that the unauthorized immigrant population reached an all-time high of 14 million in 2023, which was 27% of all U.S. immigrants.
anchor: The number of unauthorized immigrants in the United States reached an all-time high of 14 million in 2023 after two consecutive years of record growth
In 2023, unauthorized immigrants accounted for 27% of all U.S. immigrants, up from 22% in 2021.
context: Pew Research Center (nonpartisan), Passel and Krogstad, 2025-08-21, from ACS data. 2023 is the latest year with a full detailed estimate. Pew counts people with parole, pending asylum, TPS and DACA as unauthorized.

statement: Pew said that in 2025 the unauthorized immigrant population has probably started to decline, though as of mid-2025 it likely remains above 2023 levels.
anchor: In 2025, the unauthorized immigrant population has probably started to decline, due in part to increased deportations and reduced protections under the Trump administration.
As of mid-2025, the unauthorized immigrant population likely remains above 2023 levels.
context: Pew, preliminary and based on incomplete 2024-25 data. This is the early estimate of decline; later estimates (CIS, EV-IMM-011) are larger and from a restrictionist group. Pew's lead author cautioned that falling survey response rates may affect the size of the decline (reported secondhand; not checked on Pew's page).

statement: Pew reported that the U.S. immigrant population reached more than 53 million in January 2025 and fell by more than 1 million by June 2025, based on Current Population Survey data.
anchor: The overall U.S. immigrant population reached an all-time high of more than 53 million in January 2025, accounting for a record 15.8% of the U.S. population.
the number declined by more than 1 million between January and June 2025, according to data from the Current Population Survey.
context: Pew analysis of CPS monthly data; the Census Bureau cautions that CPS sample sizes are small for foreign-born estimates and the CPS has had falling response rates. Counts all immigrants, not only unauthorized. The CRS figure from the ACS (50.2 million in 2024, EV-IMM-015) is a different survey and year.

statement: MPI estimated that the unauthorized population reached 13.7 million as of mid-2023, and that 45 percent of it had lived in the country for 20 years or more.
anchor: the Migration Policy Institute (MPI) estimating it reached 13.7 million as of mid-2023, following more than a decade of stagnation. Still, nearly half of this population—45 percent—had lived in the country for 20 years or more, with 80 percent having at least five years of residence.
context: MPI (nonpartisan, pro-immigration-leaning), Oct 2025. Method assigns legal status in ACS using SIPP and DHS data. MPI later published a mid-2024 estimate of 15.8 million (July 2026 report; seen only through news and CRS, not read). This is the only length-of-residence breakdown located; a 10+ year share was not stated in the fact sheet text read.

statement: MPI estimated that as many as 4 million people, 29 percent of the unauthorized population, held TPS or DACA, had a pending asylum application, or had an active grant of humanitarian parole in mid-2023.
anchor: as of mid-2023, as many as 4 million people—29 percent of the unauthorized population—were holders of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) or Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA), had a pending asylum application, or had an active grant of humanitarian parole.
context: MPI, Oct 2025. The "quasi-legal" group. Pew counts a larger "some protection from deportation" group (about 6 million, 2023) including those released at the border (EV-IMM-009). Many of these protections ended in 2025-26 (EV-IMM-019 to EV-IMM-022).

statement: MPI estimated that 6.3 million children under 18 lived with at least one unauthorized parent, and 5.3 million of them were U.S. citizens.
anchor: At the national level, 6.3 million children under age 18 lived with at least one unauthorized immigrant parent. Of these children, the great majority—5.3 million—were U.S. citizens.
context: MPI, Oct 2025, ACS-based. Pew gives a narrower figure (EV-IMM-010: 4.6 million US-born children). The two count different things (all children with an unauthorized parent vs. US-born children), so they are not in conflict.

statement: MPI estimated that of 13 million unauthorized immigrants aged 16 and older in 2023, about 9.6 million were in the labor force.
anchor: Of the 13 million unauthorized immigrants who were ages 16 and older in 2023, about 9.6 million were in the labor force, meaning they were employed or seeking employment. Ninety-four percent were employed.
context: MPI, Oct 2025, ACS-based. Pew reports unauthorized immigrants as 5.6% of the workforce in 2023 (EV-IMM-010).

statement: Pew counted about 6 million immigrants without full legal status who had some protection from deportation in 2023, up from 2.7 million in 2021.
anchor: About 6 million immigrants without full legal status had some protection from deportation in 2023, up from 2.7 million in 2021.
Asylum applicants (2.6 million)
Temporary Protected Status (TPS), which is available to migrants in the U.S. from countries facing war, natural disasters or other crises (650,000)
context: Pew, 2025-08-21. Includes 2.6 million asylum applicants, 700,000 parolees, 650,000 TPS holders, 600,000 DACA enrollees and others; also notes that the administration in 2025 removed protections for about 500,000 CHNV parolees (Pew's description of the policy; the litigation is not verified here).
locator: section "Which groups of U.S. unauthorized immigrants had deportation protection in 2023?"

statement: Pew estimated that about 4.6 million U.S.-born children under 18 lived with an unauthorized parent in 2023, and that unauthorized immigrants were 5.6% of the U.S. workforce.

Unauthorized immigrants represented 5.6% of the U.S. workforce in 2023, a new high.
context: Pew, 2025-08-21. Quotations came from a page-fetch summary and a search extract, not the full page text; reviewer to confirm wording. Pew also reports 4.3 million unauthorized adults had lived in the U.S. 18 years or more (same extract).
locator: report sections on children and workforce (web page)

statement: The Center for Immigration Studies estimated 13.5 million illegal immigrants in July 2026, down 2.3 million, or 14.6 percent, from 15.8 million in January 2025.
anchor: we estimate that 13.5 million illegal immigrants live in the U.S. as of July 2026, down from 15.8 million when President Trump began his second term in January 2025.
this marks an extraordinary decline of 2.3 million, or 14.6 percent, in the illegal immigrant population since January 2025.
context: Center for Immigration Studies (restrictionist), 2026-09-14. Residual method on Census CPS; authors say methodological choices could move the number by a million or two. CIS counts parolees and asylum applicants as illegal. Pew (EV-IMM-003) and MPI (EV-IMM-012) give a more cautious picture; CMS has criticized use of CPS for this purpose (reported in news, not read).

statement: MPI estimated between 790,000 and 1.9 million total departures of immigrants with at least a year of residence since the start of the second Trump term, while DHS officials claimed more than 3 million.
anchor: MPI estimates that there were likely between 790,000 and 1.9 million total departures of immigrants with at least one year of U.S. residence (via deportation or self-departure)
DHS officials have claimed more than 3 million total departures
context: MPI (Rosenblum), 2026. MPI notes DHS stopped detailed enforcement reporting after January 2025, so its estimates are built from public data. The DHS figure is the second Trump administration's own claim and counts self-departures with no stated method; it must not carry a claim alone.

statement: MPI estimated about 980,000 DHS deportations between January 20, 2025 and July 31, 2026, of which 20 percent involved a person with a criminal conviction.
anchor: DHS (ICE and CBP combined) completed about 980,000 deportations, a figure in line with the department's public statements.
just 20 percent (190,000) of the 980,000 deportations carried out between January 20, 2025, and July 31, 2026, were of people who had been convicted of a crime.
context: MPI built this from public DHS data; it counts removals and returns, including about 340,000 border turnarounds. 69 percent of deportations began with border interception. DHS data are the administration's; MPI notes reporting gaps.

statement: MPI found that among deportations of immigrants with two or more years of U.S. residence, 71 percent were of people who had never been convicted of a crime.
anchor: Of total deportations of immigrants with two or more years of U.S. residence, 71 percent (280,000) were of people who had never been convicted of a crime
context: MPI (Rosenblum), from public DHS data; 61 percent of ICE deportations excluding border turnarounds were of people present at least two years and 15 percent of people present ten or more years.

anchor: In 2024, according to the American Community Survey ( ACS ) , an estimated 50.2 million foreign-born people resided in the United States, representing approximately 14.8% of the total U.S. population
context: CRS (nonpartisan) restating ACS Table B05001. The ACS does not ask about status. Pew's 53 million (Jan 2025, CPS) is a different survey (EV-IMM-004).

anchor: As of June 30, 2026, 436,350 individuals were covered by DACA, which is granted to certain persons brought to the United States as children.

context: CRS quoting the statute. The CRS note says H.R. 1689, passed by the House on 2026-04-16, would require Haiti's designation until 3 months after January 20, 2029, and that Congress could amend the review bar. Whether the Senate acts is open.

recorded less than 99,000 southwest border apprehensions in FY 2026

statement: CBO and JCT estimated that the committee-approved Border Security, Economic Opportunity, and Immigration Modernization Act would decrease federal budget deficits by $197 billion over 2014-2023 and by roughly $700 billion over 2024-2033, not counting a further limited set of economic effects.
anchor: the cost estimate shows that changes in direct spending and revenues under the legislation would decrease federal budget deficits by $197 billion over the 2014–2023 period and by roughly $700 billion over the 2024–2033 period.
locator: Report summary, "How Would the Economic Impact of the Legislation Affect Federal Budget Deficits?"
context: Score of the Judiciary Committee version (reported May 28, 2013, star print June 6), published June 18, 2013. Dynamic effects not in the estimate were expected to cut deficits by about $300 billion more in the second decade (EV-IMM-201). The legacy file's "about $175B first-decade deficit cut" is widely reported for CBO's June 24, 2013 preliminary letter on the bill as amended by Corker-Hoeven. The quoted letter text (EV-IMM-207) says less than $40B below $197B. The $175B is not confirmed from CBO's text. The final estimate for the Senate-passed bill is $158B (EV-IMM-205).

statement: CBO's central estimates were that the economic impacts not in the cost estimate would have no further net effect on deficits over 2014-2023 and would reduce deficits by about $300 billion more over 2024-2033.
anchor: the economic impacts not included in the cost estimate would have no further net effect on budget deficits over the 2014–2023 period and would further reduce deficits (relative to the effects reported in the cost estimate) by about $300 billion over the 2024–2033 period.
context: The range reflects uncertainty about two key economic relationships. CBO said projecting beyond 20 years was not attempted.

statement: CBO estimated S. 744 would raise real GDP by 3.3 percent in 2023 and by 5.4 percent in 2033, relative to current law, while lowering per capita GNP by 0.7 percent in 2023 and raising it by 0.2 percent in 2033.

S. 744 would lower per capita GNP by 0.7 percent in 2023 and raise it by 0.2 percent in 2033
locator: Report, "How Would the Legislation Affect the Economy?"
context: Most of the GDP gain comes from a larger labor force; the bill included large legal-immigration and guest-worker expansions, so the figure is not a legalization-only effect. The bill's GDP effect is relative to a CBO 2013 baseline with much lower immigration than today.

statement: CBO estimated the Senate immigration bill would raise the U.S. population by about 10 million people in 2023 and about 16 million in 2033, and the labor force by about 6 million in 2023 and about 9 million in 2033.
anchor: enacting the bill would, in CBO’s view, increase the U.S. population by about 10 million people (about 3 percent) in 2023 and by about 16 million people (about 4 percent) in 2033.
the size of the labor force by about 6 million (about 3½ percent) in 2023 and by about 9 million (about 5 percent) in 2033
context: The population increase combines legalization, new legal admissions and children born to new entrants, minus lower unauthorized inflows. It is not the number of people legalized. The same CBO files put the Senate-passed net increase at 9.6 million by 2023 (EV-IMM-206).

statement: CBO estimated average wages for the entire labor force would be 0.1 percent lower in 2023 and 0.5 percent higher in 2033 under the Senate immigration bill than under current law, and that the unemployment rate would be slightly higher through 2020.

Slightly raise the unemployment rate through 2020

context: CBO also said wages of lower- and higher-skilled workers would be pushed down slightly (by less than one-half percent) relative to workers with average skills. CBO did not analyze the incomes of people who would be residents under current law separately, so the average-wage dip partly reflects lower-wage new residents.

statement: CBO and JCT estimated that the Senate-passed Border Security, Economic Opportunity, and Immigration Modernization Act would decrease federal deficits by $158 billion over 2014-2023, with net discretionary costs of $23 billion, for net savings of about $135 billion.

net discretionary costs of $23 billion over the 2014-2023 period
a net savings of about $135 billion over the 2014-2023 period

Relative to the committee bill, the Senate-passed bill raised direct spending by about $36 billion and cut revenues by about $3 billion over the decade. statement: CBO estimated that enacting S. 744 as passed would lead to a net increase of 9.6 million in the total number of people residing in the United States by 2023.

context: Net of reduced unauthorized inflows. The increase in legal residents would raise direct spending for federal benefit programs; revenue is higher mostly from the larger labor force (same paragraph).

statement: CBO said the Corker-Hoeven substitute amendment to the Senate immigration bill would appropriate $46.3 billion for southern-border security and initial administrative costs, $38 billion more than the committee bill, so the 10-year deficit reduction would be smaller than the committee bill's $197 billion by less than $40 billion.

10-year savings would be smaller than the $197 billion projected for the committee-approved bill by something less than $40 billion.

statement: CBO said enacting the Corker-Hoeven substitute amendment would increase on-budget deficits over 2014-2023 because much of the expected revenue gain would come from Social Security payroll taxes, which are off-budget.

statement: CBO estimated that the 2006 Senate immigration bill, would increase direct spending by $48 billion over 2007-2016 and increase discretionary spending by $78 billion over the same period, and would reduce revenues by about $79 billion as written or increase them by about $44 billion if a tax exemption were read as intended.

enacting this legislation would increase direct spending by $16 billion over the 2007-2011 period and by $48 billion over the 2007-2016 period.

the act would increase revenues by about $44 billion over the 2007-2016 period

context: Biden-era surge; CBO later revised net immigration sharply down for 2025 onward (January 2026 demographic outlook, not read directly). The category includes people with and without permission to stay.

statement: CBO estimated that the recent immigration surge lowers deficits by $0.9 trillion over 2024-2034, with $1.2 trillion more in federal revenues and $0.3 trillion more in mandatory outlays and net interest.
anchor: lowering deficits, on net, by $0.9 trillion over the 2024–2034 period
CBO estimates that the immigration surge will add $1.2 trillion in federal revenues over the 2024–2034 period.
The immigration surge adds $0.3 trillion to outlays for federal mandatory programs and net spending for interest on the debt
context: This is CBO's most recent whole-economy fiscal score of a large immigrant inflow, and it excludes discretionary spending and state and local budgets. It is about all immigrants in the surge, mostly not legalized, so it is a rough comparator, not a legalization score.

statement: CBO wrote that research has generally found increases in immigration raise state and local governments' costs more than their revenues, and that it expected this to hold for the current surge.
anchor: Research has generally found that increases in immigration raise state and local governments’ costs more than their revenues, and CBO expects that finding to hold in the case of the current immigration surge.
context: CBO did not fully analyze state and local effects in this report; its separate 2025 analysis is in the library as SRC-0416. Consistent with the National Academies finding by level of government (EV-IMM-222).

statement: The National Academies panel (2017) found that over a long horizon of 75 years the fiscal impacts of immigrants are generally positive at the federal level and negative at the state and local levels.
anchor: Viewed over a long time horizon (75 years in our estimates), the fiscal impacts of immigrants are generally positive at the federal level and negative at the state and local levels.
context: Consensus panel; the finding turns on counting the children of immigrants and on assumptions about future debt. Not about legalization specifically; unauthorized immigrants are a minority of the foreign-born. Panel funded by foundations and agencies; study published during the first Trump administration.

statement: The National Academies panel found that, measured over more than 10 years, the impact of immigration on the wages of natives overall is very small, and that to the extent negative wage effects are found, prior immigrants and native-born high school dropouts are most likely to experience them.
anchor: When measured over a period of more than 10 years, the impact of immigration on the wages of natives overall is very small.

To the extent that negative wage effects are found, prior immigrants—who are often the closest substitutes for new immigrants—are most likely to experience them, followed by native-born high school dropouts
context: Panel review of the empirical literature. The finding frames the restrictionist and expansionist estimates (EV-IMM-225, EV-IMM-226) and CBO's wage figure (EV-IMM-204).

statement: The National Academies panel found that individuals in the first generation are more costly to governments, mainly at the state and local levels, than the native-born, while the second generation are among the strongest economic and fiscal contributors.
anchor: On average, individuals in the first generation are more costly to governments, mainly at the state and local levels, than are the native-born generations; however, immigrants’ children—the second generation—are among the strongest economic and fiscal contributors in the population.
context: Cross-sectional finding, 1994-2013 CPS data. Estimates of long-run impact would likely be more positive if labor force growth and innovation effects were counted (same section).

statement: Penn Wharton Budget Model estimated a 10-year mass deportation policy would raise primary deficits by about $862 billion before economic feedback and $987 billion with it, and cut GDP by 3.3 percent by 2034.
anchor: The 10-year policy would cost about $862 billion before economic feedback effects and $987 billion with economic feedback effects.
By 2034, the 4-year policy reduces GDP by 1.0 percent; the 10-year policy reduces it by 3.3 percent.
context: University model brief, July 25, 2025, in the second Trump administration, which disputed it. The costs are on top of the about $170 billion already allocated in the 2025 reconciliation law. Scenario: 10 percent of unauthorized immigrants removed per year.

statement: The American Immigration Council estimated a one-time mass deportation operation would cost at least $315 billion, and a yearslong operation would cost $88 billion a year, totaling $967.9 billion over 10.6 years.
anchor: A one-time operation to deport these immigrants would cost at least $315 billion
the ultimate cost of such a longer operation would average out to $88 billion annually, for a total cost of $967.9 billion over the course of more than a decade.
The total cost over 10.6 years (assuming an annual inflation rate of 2.5 percent) would be $967.9 billion.
context: Advocacy group estimate, October 2, 2024. Targets about 13.3 million people (11 million unauthorized plus 2.3 million released) and assumes 20 percent self-deport in the longer scenario. Not a CBO figure; CBO has no estimate that this research found.

statement: Penn Wharton found that under a 10-year deportation policy high-skilled workers' wages fall by 2.8 percent ($2,764 a year) while wages of authorized low-skilled workers rise by 5.0 percent by 2034.
anchor: by 2.8 percent or $2,764 for the 10-year policy
Under the 10-year policy, their wages increase by 5.0 percent by 2034 and mostly persist thereafter.
context: Shows the distributional split behind aggregate wage claims: removal helps low-skilled authorized workers and hurts high-skilled workers in this model. Reversal after four years leaves low-income workers worse off over time (same section).

statement: ITEP estimated undocumented immigrants paid $96.7 billion in federal, state and local taxes in 2022, of which $59.4 billion went to the federal government and $37.3 billion to states and localities.
anchor: Undocumented immigrants paid $96.7 billion in federal, state, and local taxes in 2022. Most of that amount, $59.4 billion, was paid to the federal government while the remaining $37.3 billion was paid to state and local governments.
context: Microsimulation by a left-leaning tax group, July 2024; population 10.9 million in 2022. The same report models a work-authorization scenario (EV-IMM-229). Social Security taxes of $25.7 billion are paid into programs these workers cannot draw on.

statement: ITEP estimated that granting work authorization to undocumented immigrants would raise their total tax payments to $136.9 billion a year, of which $33.1 billion more would go to the federal government and $7.1 billion more to states and localities.
anchor: 136.9 billion. Most of the new revenue raised in this scenario ($33.1 billion) would flow to the federal government while the remainder ($7.1 billion) would flow to states and localities.
context: A static scenario (ITEP's own microsimulation, not a CBO/JCT score); it ignores benefit costs, which CBO's H.R. 6 and H.R. 1603 scores show offset much of the revenue (EV-IMM-213, EV-IMM-215).

statement: Kossoudji and Cobb-Clark estimated the wage penalty for being unauthorized at 14 to 24 percent and the wage benefit of legalization under IRCA at about 6 percent, in a sample of legalized men.
anchor: The 1986 Immigration Reform and Control Act (IRCA) granted amnesty to approximately 1.7 million long-term unauthorized workers
The wage penalty for being unauthorized is estimated to range from 14% to 24%. The wage benefit of legalization under IRCA was approximately 6%.
context: Peer-reviewed; panel data on legalized men from the 1990s with a comparison group. The 1.7 million is the paper's own count of long-term unauthorized workers; other sources say nearly 3 million (EV-IMM-233, EV-IMM-234).

statement: Orrenius and Zavodny found that apprehensions at the Mexican border fell right after IRCA passed but returned to normal levels when amnesty applications were being filed, and concluded that the amnesty did not change long-run patterns of illegal immigration from Mexico.
anchor: which granted amnesty to over 3 million undocumented immigrants

apprehensions of persons attempting to illegally cross the U.S.-Mexico border declined immediately following passage of the law but returned to normal levels during the period when illegal immigrants could file for amnesty and the years thereafter.
the amnesty program did not change long-run patterns of illegal immigration from Mexico.
context: Working-paper version (2001); later published in Demography, 2003, where the title reads as a question. The paper tests whether legalization draws more unauthorized entry; it says nothing about the separate effect of employer sanctions or border enforcement increases after 1986.

statement: Baker found that IRCA, which legalized almost 3 million immigrants, reduced crime by 3 to 5 percent, mostly property crime, equal to 120,000-180,000 fewer crimes a year, and that much of the drop is explained by better labor market opportunities.
anchor: IRCA), which legalized almost 3 million immigrants
I find decreases in crime of 3-5 percent, primarily due to decline in property crimes, equivalent to 120,000-180,000 fewer violent and property crimes committed each year due to legalization.
context: Peer-reviewed (AER Papers and Proceedings, short paper); uses quasi-random timing and variation in treatment intensity across places. The result is for 1986-era crime and applicants.

statement: Pope found that DACA, which offered relief to 1.7 million unauthorized immigrants, increased the likelihood of working by raising labor force participation and lowering unemployment, and moved 50,000 to 75,000 into employment.
anchor: made deportation relief and work authorization available to 1.7 million unauthorized immigrants.
DACA increases the likelihood of working by increasing labor force participation and decreasing the unemployment rate for DACA-eligible immigrants.
DACA moved 50,000 to 75,000 unauthorized immigrants into employment.
context: Peer-reviewed; difference-in-differences near the eligibility cutoffs. DACA gave work authorization and deportation relief but no path to a green card, so it is closer to the "status only" design (legacy option IMM-1C) than to a green-card path.

statement: Hainmueller and co-authors found that mothers' DACA eligibility significantly decreased adjustment and anxiety disorder diagnoses among their U.S.-citizen children, using Oregon Medicaid claims.
anchor: The Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program granted temporary protection from deportation to more than 780,000 unauthorized immigrants.
Mothers' DACA eligibility significantly decreased adjustment and anxiety disorder diagnoses among their children.
context: Peer-reviewed in Science; a regression discontinuity on the DACA age cutoff using Emergency Medicaid births in Oregon. The study cannot identify the mechanism.

statement: GAO reported in 1990 that, because of IRCA's employer sanctions, about 10 percent of employers began one or more discriminatory practices, and that 65 percent of employers reported compliance.
anchor: (4) because of the law, about 10 percent of employers began one or more discriminatory practices
65 percent of employers reported that they complied with IRCA
context: Third and final annual GAO report required by IRCA section 101(a), based on employer surveys. GAO's overall answer to Congress on discrimination was yes, per the report. The Immigration Act of 1990 added anti-discrimination provisions. Quotation from a mirror of the GAO page; reviewer to confirm wording on gao.gov.

statement: NPR reported that the Senate parliamentarian ruled against Democrats' third attempt to include immigration provisions in the Build Back Better reconciliation bill, after two earlier rulings in September, the first on a pathway to citizenship for 8 million immigrants.
anchor: MacDonough has ruled against Democrats' pitch to include immigration reform provisions in their almost $2 trillion social spending bill, in a major setback for the party in their third attempt
In September, MacDonough ruled against Democrats in two previous efforts to include immigration reform plans
Plan A," Democrats proposed a pathway to citizenship for 8 million immigrants
context: News account; the parliamentarian's written rulings are not published in the sources tried. The third plan would have given work permits to people in the U.S. since before 2011 (NPR). The three-rejection count, "Plan A" (citizenship), "Plan B" (registry date) and the third (parole and work permits), matches the legacy file's memory. Rulings are advisory; the Senate did not overrule them.

statement: The March 2022 DHS and DOJ interim final rule lets USCIS asylum officers consider the asylum claims of people found to have a credible fear through a nonadversarial merits interview.
anchor:
through a
nonadversarial merits interview
conducted by an asylum officer when
such application is retained by USCIS
context: Biden-administration rule, 87 FR 18078, published 2022-03-29. It is an interim final rule; the section anchored is the Departments' summary of the third major change. Status after 2025: see EV-IMM-304 and EV-IMM-305.

statement: The 2022 rule requires the asylum officer to hold the merits interview within 45 days of service of the positive credible fear determination.
anchor:
The asylum officer shall
conduct the interview within 45 days of
the date that the positive credible fear
determination is served on the
noncitizen
context: Regulatory text as described in the preamble; the rule was implemented in phases (EV-IMM-303), so actual timelines differed.

statement: DHS estimated in 2022 that fully implementing the asylum officer merits process would need about 800 new employees and about $180 million for about 75,000 cases a year.
anchor:
approximately 800 new employees
and spend approximately $180 million
to fully implement the proposed
Asylum Merits interview and
adjudication process to handle
approximately 75,000 cases annually
context: Agency staffing and cost estimate in the Biden-administration preamble; a projection, not an outcome. The same preamble says addressing the affirmative backlog was outside the scope of the rule.

statement: USCIS began implementing the asylum officer rule in a phased way, starting with a few hundred referrals a month for merits interviews.
anchor:
starting with the referral of a few hundred aliens each
month for asylum merits interviews
context: CRS summary in July 2022, early in implementation; it does not report later case counts. I could not retrieve USCIS merits-interview totals (see notes).

statement: A Federal Register rule of late 2025 lists the Asylum Processing IFR among four later rules that amended the credible fear provisions.
anchor:
the Departments have
issued four rules amending their
credible fear provisions that are relevant
here: (1) the Asylum Processing IFR
context: Second Trump administration rule. Establishes only that the 2022 IFR was treated as an existing rule in December 2025. I found no Federal Register document rescinding it, but absence of a rescission in my search is not proof; reviewer should check the eCFR for 8 CFR 208.9 and 208.30.

statement: A July 2026 DHS interim final rule, effective July 28, 2026, lets USCIS refer certain affirmative asylum applications to the immigration courts without an interview.
anchor:
Effective date: This interim final rule
(IFR) is effective July 28, 2026
context: Second Trump administration rule (91 FR 47101). It changes the affirmative track, not the 2022 expedited-removal merits process, but moves the system away from interviewing every applicant. Litigation not checked.

statement: DHS said that by the end of fiscal year 2025 over 1.4 million affirmative asylum applications were pending at USCIS, after receipts reached a high of 465,810 in 2023.
anchor:
reaching a high of 465,810 in
2023. See Table 5. By the end of FY
2025, over 1.4 million affirmative
asylum applications remained pending
at USCIS
context: Counts come from the 2026 DHS rule under the second Trump administration, which uses them to justify the rule; USCIS administrative counts, definition of pending not independently checked.

statement: DHS estimates about 132,167 future affirmative asylum applicants a year and up to 444,724 pending applicants could be referred without interview.
anchor:
approximately 132,167
aliens seeking affirmative asylum
annually may be referred without
interview
Potentially, up to 444,724
context: Second Trump administration DHS estimate of rule reach; administration analysis does not carry a claim alone.

statement: DHS acknowledged that its 2026 no-interview rule will initially increase referrals to the immigration courts and could increase their pending caseload.
anchor:
it will initially increase the
volume of USCIS referrals to EOIR
annually, which could then increase
EOIR’s pending cases backlog
context: Second Trump administration DHS admission in the preamble. Useful as an admitted cost of moving cases from asylum officers to judges.

statement: In fiscal year 2023 the immigration courts issued 492,981 initial case decisions, and the most common was a removal order, at 47 percent.
anchor:
EOIR issued 492,981 initial case decisions (parties may file an appeal). The most common
decision was issuance of a removal order (47%)
context: EOIR data summarized by CRS; fiscal year 2023 (Biden administration). Dismissals and terminations together were 42 percent.

statement: Of 231,095 removal orders issued in fiscal year 2023, 69 percent, or 159,379, were issued in absentia.
anchor:
Among the 231,095 total removal orders issued in FY2023 (Figure 1), 69% (159,379) were in absentia
removal orders
context: CRS notes that how to measure failure to appear is debated: EOIR divides in absentia orders by initial completions, while others argue the 2.5 million pending cases (end of FY2023) should be considered. See EV-IMM-315.

statement: Immigration judges decided 51,607 asylum cases in fiscal year 2022, up from 24,810, and granted asylum to 23,686 people, the most in the court's history.
anchor: Total decisions more than doubled from 24,810 in FY 2021, to 51,607 during FY 2022. And the number of individuals granted asylum by Immigration Judges increased from 8,945 to 23,686.
context: TRAC analysis of EOIR records, fiscal year 2022. Merits decisions only; does not include grants by USCIS asylum officers.

statement: Of affirmative asylum cases that asylum officers had rejected, 76 percent were granted asylum on rehearing by immigration judges in fiscal year 2022, against 39 percent of defensive cases.
anchor: Over three-quarters (76%) of cases USCIS asylum officers had rejected were granted asylum on rehearing by Immigration Judges. Individuals who brought asylum claims as a defense against being deported won asylum just 39 percent of the time.
locator: report text, "Affirmative vs Defensive Asylum Cases"
context: TRAC. The comparison is of two different populations (cases referred after USCIS denial versus defensive cases) and excludes cases USCIS granted, so it is not a measure of officer error.

statement: Only 37 percent of immigrants in over 1.2 million removal cases decided between 2007 and 2012 secured representation, and just 14 percent of detained immigrants.
anchor: Drawing on data from over 1.2 million deportation cases decided between 2007 and 2012, we find that only 37% of all immigrants, and a mere 14% of detained immigrants, secured representation
context: Peer-reviewed national study; the data predate the post-2014 surge and later representation rates are likely different (a 2025 follow-up by the same authors is reported but not read).

statement: Among similarly situated respondents, the odds of seeking relief were fifteen times greater, and of obtaining relief five-and-a-half times greater, with a lawyer.
anchor: the odds were fifteen times greater that immigrants with representation, as compared to those without, sought relief, and five-and-a-half times greater that they obtained relief from removal
context: Regression-adjusted odds ratios from observational data, not randomized; peer-reviewed. Counsel may be chosen by people with stronger cases despite controls.

statement: Eighty-three percent of non-detained immigrants with removal cases from 2008 to 2018 attended all their hearings, and 96 percent of those with a lawyer did.
anchor: 83% of all nondetained immigrants with completed or pending removal cases from Fiscal Years (FY) 2008 through 2018 attended all of their court hearings. Among those who were represented by counsel during the same time period, 96% attended all of their court hearings.
context: Authors' analysis of EOIR data obtained from the government; published by an advocacy organization, though the underlying article is peer-reviewed. Contrasts with the in absentia share of removal orders (EV-IMM-310), which uses a different denominator.

statement: Fifteen percent of removal orders issued for failure to appear from 2008 to 2018 were later overturned.
anchor: 15% of all removal orders for failure to appear issued from 2008 to 2018 were successfully overturned
context: Same source and caveats as EV-IMM-315.

statement: In the first cases completed on the Los Angeles Dedicated Docket by February 2022, 99.1 percent of the 449 ended in removal orders, and 72.4 percent of those were in absentia.
anchor: 99.1% of the 449 cases com
context: Los Angeles only and an early snapshot of completed cases, which skew toward quick in absentia orders; a clinic study. National Dedicated Docket results were not retrieved.

statement: MPI's 2018 report called for managing the Asylum Division's resources so that eligible applicants could get protection within the six-month statutory standard.
anchor: applicants eligible for protection can get it within six months, the statutory standard, while also deterring misuse
locator: Section V.B, Recommendations to Restore Order and Build Resilience
context: Think-tank recommendation written under the first Trump administration. The newer MPI paper on asylum officer adjudication (2026) was found in search but not read, so this is only the earlier position.

statement: DHS projected in July 2026 that people seeking affirmative asylum may wait over 7.3 years for resolution if nothing changes.
anchor:
individuals
seeking asylum may wait over 7.3 years
for resolution
context: Second Trump administration DHS projection from receipts and pending counts; a method note for the figure was not read. Administration analysis does not carry a claim alone.

statement: The immigration courts had 2.5 million pending removal cases at the end of fiscal year 2023.
anchor: (2.5 million at the end of FY2023)
context: EOIR count as relayed by CRS; later counts not retrieved here (TRAC and EOIR publish current totals).

statement: Human Rights First reported that 40 percent of people whose cases the USCIS Asylum Office decided on the claim were granted asylum in calendar year 2022 through September, down from 44 percent in fiscal year 2016.
anchor: 40 percent of people whose cases were decided by the USCIS Asylum Office based on their asylum claim were granted asylum
in FY 2016, 44 percent of people whose cases were decided by USCIS on the merits were granted asylum
context: Advocacy group analysis of USCIS data. This is the affirmative Asylum Office rate, NOT the 2022-rule Asylum Merits Interview track: the page does not mention that process. No source I could open gave merits-interview counts, grant rates or timelines for credible-fear cases. Quotation from a fetch extract; reviewer to confirm wording.

statement: Human Rights First reported that in fiscal years 2022 and 2023, 76 percent of cases referred to immigration court by USCIS were granted asylum there.
anchor: In FYs 2022 and 2023, 76 percent of all cases that were referred to immigration court by USCIS were granted asylum
context: Matches the TRAC figure of 76 percent for FY2022 (EV-IMM-312); both describe cases the Asylum Office did not grant, so the group is selected. Quotation from a fetch extract; reviewer to confirm wording.

statement: From 2013 to 2024, 52 percent of immigrants in completed removal cases found counsel, including 62 percent of unaccompanied children, up from 37 percent in 2007 to 2012.
anchor: While only 37% of immigrants in completed removal cases found counsel in our initial study (from 2007 to 2012), just over half found counsel (52%) in the subsequent years (from 2013 to 2024), including 62% of unaccompanied children.
context: Peer-reviewed-style law review revisit of EV-IMM-313 by the same authors; unaccompanied children are a subgroup with federally funded counsel until 2025 (the paper notes the administration tried to stop that funding).

statement: Representation among detained immigrants rose from 14 percent to 31 percent, while representation of non-detained immigrants fell from 66 percent to 57 percent, between the original and the later period.
anchor: representation for detained immigrants increased from 14% to 31%, representation for immigrants who were not detained decreased from 66% to 57%
locator: Part on representation by custody status, Figure 8a
context: Same study as EV-IMM-323; periods are 2007-2012 versus 2013-2024. Falling non-detained representation is the strain the authors flag.

statement: In fiscal year 2024, 16,976 representatives provided counsel for just over 1.4 million immigrants facing removal, leaving almost 2.9 million unrepresented.
anchor: In fiscal year 2024, only 16,976 representatives provided counsel for just over 1.4 million immigrants facing removal, leaving almost 2.9 million immigrants unrepresented.
context: The authors' count from EOIR administrative data (supplied through TRAC). Counts people in pending and completed cases; a derived total, so treat as an estimate.

statement: Almost two-thirds (64 percent) of immigrants who found counsel succeeded in avoiding deportation, such as with a grant of asylum or termination of their case.
anchor: almost two-thirds (64%) of immigrants who found counsel succeeded in avoiding deportation, such as with a grant of asylum or termination of their case
context: Descriptive rate for represented respondents, not a causal estimate; the earlier regression result is EV-IMM-314.

statement: Vera projected that 48 percent of New York Immigrant Family Unity Project cases would end successfully, against a 4 percent success rate for unrepresented cases at Varick Street before the program.
anchor: Vera has projected that 48 percent of cases will end successfully for NYIFUP clients. This is a 1,100 percent increase from the 4 percent success rate for unrepresented cases at Varick Street before NYIFUP.
context: 48 percent is a model projection for pending cases, compared with a pre-program baseline at one New York detained court, so selection and timing differences remain. The program funder is New York City.

statement: NYIFUP clients obtained bond and release from detention at close to double the rate of similar unrepresented people at comparable courts, 49 percent against 25 percent.
anchor: 49 percent for NYIFUP versus 25 percent for unrepresented individuals at similar courts
context: Vera comparison with similarly situated cases at other courts; observational.

statement: EOIR's 2019 analysis found Legal Orientation Program participants averaged 106 days in detention against 76 days for non-participants, about 30 more days and an estimated $3,700 more per person.
anchor:
LOP respondents averaging
106 days in detention and non-LOP respondents averaging 76 days in detention.

LOP participants on average spent 30 more days in detention than non-LOP participants,
which results in an estimated additional $3,700 in detention costs per LOP respondent.
context: First Trump administration analysis that ran against earlier findings (Vera 2008 and a 2012 EOIR analysis reported shorter cases and detention for participants, per search summaries I could not open). The report itself warns that other factors, such as hearing location, may contribute. Vera disputed the method (not verified from Vera).

statement: ICE's Alternatives to Detention enrollment more than doubled from approximately 53,000 in 2015 to 111,000 in 2020, GAO found.
anchor: more than doubled from approximately 53,000 in 2015 to 111,000 in 2020
context: GAO analysis of ICE contractor data. Enrollment since then has grown much further (EV-IMM-358).

statement: GAO found ICE unenrolled most participants before their immigration proceedings ended, placing about half on monitoring outside the program while about a quarter absconded.
anchor: ICE placed about half of unenrolled participants on monitoring outside of the ATD program and about a quarter absconded
context: GAO also notes ICE does not include all relevant participants when calculating absconsion rates (EV-IMM-353), so the quarter is not a clean non-appearance rate.

statement: In March 2020 ICE awarded BI Incorporated a contract with a total value of $2.2 billion to help run the Alternatives to Detention program.
anchor: In March 2020, ICE awarded a contract with a total value of $2.2 billion to BI Incorporated
context: Contract ceiling, not annual spending.

statement: GAO said ICE does not include all relevant participants when calculating absconsion rates for its Alternatives to Detention program.
anchor: ICE does not include all relevant participants when calculating absconsion rates
context: GAO recommended better external reporting of absconsion information; DHS concurred. Whether ICE has since fixed this was not checked.

statement: In the three fiscal years GAO reviewed, over 99 percent of people in the full-service component of ICE's program with a scheduled hearing appeared in court, but ICE did not collect similar data for the technology-only component, 39 percent of participants.
anchor: these data showed that over 99 percent of aliens with a scheduled court hearing appeared in court as required
which composed 39 percent of the overall ATD program participants in fiscal year 2013
context: GAO audit of Obama-era data. The full-service group was a selected, case-managed population, so 99 percent should not be read as the rate for all released people.

statement: In fiscal year 2016 the Family Case Management Program cost about $38.47 per family a day, against $237.60 a day for family detention and about $4.40 per person for ISAP III.
anchor: The FCMP cost approximately $38.47 per family per day in FY2016, versus approximately $4.40 per person per day for ISAP III. By comparison, family detention costs an estimated $237.60
context: ICE cost figures reported by CRS in 2019. Per-family and per-person units differ; CRS notes the case-managed program cost more than electronic monitoring because of services and a more vulnerable population.

statement: The Women's Refugee Commission reported that 952 families were enrolled in the Family Case Management Program, with 99.3 percent complying with court hearings and 99.4 percent with ICE check-ins.
anchor: A total of 952 families were enrolled in FCMP
99.3% complied with immigration court hearings.
99.4% complied with ICE check-in appointments.
context: Advocacy summary relying mainly on ICE and contractor (GEO Care) final evaluations; most families had not finished their cases when ICE ended the program, so compliance was measured mid-case. A DHS OIG 2017 review of the program was not retrieved.

statement: ICE ended the Family Case Management Program in June 2017, about 1.5 years into a planned five-year program in five cities.
anchor: Although planned as a five-year program in five cities across the United States, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) terminated the program in June 2017, only 1.5 years into its implementation
context: The Commission says termination was for political reasons; that inference is the advocacy group's.

statement: ICE said that through the end of October 2024 about 7.6 million people were on its non-detained docket, of whom more than 179,000 were in the ATD-ISAP program.
anchor: Through the end of October 2024, approximately 7.6 million aliens were being overseen on ICE’s non-detained docket.
Of those, more than 179,000 participated in the ATD-ISAP program.
context: Executive-branch web page; second Trump administration period but data are from late FY2025 Q1 of the previous administration. Quotation from a fetch extract; reviewer to confirm wording. Press reporting of 182,617 enrolled in August 2025 was not verified.

statement: ICE states the daily cost per ATD-ISAP participant is less than $4.20 against about $152 a day for detention.
anchor: The daily cost per ATD-ISAP participant is less than $4.20 per day
a stark contrast from the cost of detention, which is around $152 per day.
context: ICE's own statement; the page is undated and other sources cite a different ATD figure (about $8 a day) that I could not verify. Quotation from a fetch extract; reviewer to confirm wording. Contract-only cost, excludes ICE staff.

statement: NPR reported in April 2026 that twenty-nine people had died in ICE custody since October, surpassing 2004's toll of 28 as the previous record.
anchor: Twenty-nine people have died in ICE custody since October
already surpassing 2004's toll of 28, the previous record
context: News tally partway through fiscal year 2026 (second Trump administration); a later Bloomberg item reported 37 deaths by September 30, 2026 but was seen only as a search snippet. Official ICE death reports not retrieved. Quotation from a fetch extract; reviewer to confirm wording.

statement: CRS reported that an ICE review published in March 2017 found Family Case Management compliance consistent with other ICE monitoring options but daily costs per family higher than ISAP III.
anchor: An ICE review of the program published in March 2017 showed that although the rates of compliance for the FCMP were consistent with other ICE monitoring options, FCMP daily costs per family unit were higher than ISAP III.
context: Gives the less favourable reading of the case-managed program than the Women's Refugee Commission summary (EV-IMM-356): similar compliance, higher cost than electronic monitoring, still far below detention (EV-IMM-355).

statement: ICE's FY2027 budget request includes $3.7 billion for Custody Operations, which it says sustains 41,500 detention beds.
anchor:
the FY 2027 budget includes $3.7 billion to maintain Custody
Operations. At this funding level, the FY 2027 budget sustains 41,500 detention beds.
context: Second Trump administration request, not an appropriation; the same testimony says the 2025 reconciliation law provides additional surge beds. No per-bed daily rate or ATD cost appears in the testimony; the FY2027 Congressional Budget Justification itself was not retrieved.

statement: In fiscal year 2009 the erroneous tentative nonconfirmation rate for E-Verify was 0.3 percent, down from 0.7 percent in 2005.
anchor: The erroneous TNC rate for E-Verify in FY 2009 was 0.3 percent and has been declining over time. The erroneous TNC rate declined from 0.7 to 0.3 between April through June 2005 and April through June 2010.
context: Westat evaluation for DHS. Rate counts workers found authorized after first receiving a TNC; it excludes authorized workers who got a TNC and did not contest it, so it understates error. System has changed since (photo matching, myE-Verify).

statement: The erroneous tentative nonconfirmation rate in fiscal year 2009 was 0.2 percent for U.S. citizens, 0.7 percent for permanent residents and 4.2 percent for other employment-authorized noncitizens.
anchor: In FY 2009, the erroneous TNC rate was 0.2 percent for U.S. citizens compared to 0.7 percent for permanent residents and 4.2 percent for other employment-authorized noncitizens.
context: Westat for DHS. Shows the burden of errors falls disproportionately on work-authorized noncitizens.

statement: Westat estimated that 94 percent of final nonconfirmations in fiscal year 2009 were accurately issued to unauthorized workers and 6 percent inaccurately issued to authorized workers.
anchor: It is estimated that 94 percent of FNCs were accurately issued to unauthorized workers and 6 percent were inaccurately issued to employment-authorized workers.
context: Model-based estimate (the report says validity depends on model assumptions). Government-commissioned contractor.

statement: Westat's later report restated that approximately half of unauthorized workers submitted to E-Verify were incorrectly found employment authorized, mainly through identity fraud.
anchor: the FY 2009 evaluation report indicated that approximately half of the cases submitted to E-Verify for unauthorized workers were incorrectly found to be employment authorized
Identity fraud is the major cause of employment-authorized findings being given to unauthorized workers.
context: The 2009 figure was reported by the Westat 2009 evaluation (about 54 percent in advocacy summaries; the exact 54 percent was not found in the 2012 text). Since then E-Verify added photo matching and other tools; no later accuracy study was retrieved.

statement: CBO estimated that implementing the Legal Workforce Act (H.R. 1772) would cost about $635 million over five years and increase federal deficits by about $30 billion over ten years.
anchor: CBO estimates that implementing H.R. 1772 would cost about $635 million over the 2014–
would increase budget deficits as measured by the unified Federal budget by about $30 billion over the 10-year period
context: CBO and Joint Committee on Taxation estimate of December 17, 2013 for a bill requiring all employers to use E-Verify (112th/113th Congress versions differ). A 2026 CBO item on a later E-Verify bill was found but not readable. Wage and tax effects assume off-the-books shifts.

statement: CBO and JCT estimated that mandatory E-Verify would cut off-budget Social Security payroll revenue by $88 billion and net revenue by $39 billion over ten years, as some workers move into the underground economy.
anchor: would decrease off-budget (Social Security payroll tax) revenues by about
$88 billion over that period. Thus, we estimate that the net revenue loss to the unified budget would total $39 billion over the 10year period.
they would move into the underground economy
context: JCT revenue modelling in the CBO letter; on-budget revenues were estimated to rise $49 billion because of higher business profits. A projection, not an observed outcome.

statement: As of April 2, 2018, 779,722 employers were enrolled in E-Verify, representing more than 2.5 million hiring sites.
anchor: As of April 2, 2018, there were 779,722 employers enrolled in E-Verify, representing more than 2.5 million hiring sites.
context: Dated; later enrollment (about one million in search results) was not verified from USCIS. Program remained largely voluntary at the federal level.

statement: In 2018 CRS reported that E-Verify was authorized only until September 30, 2018, through the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2018, after repeated short extensions.
anchor: It is currently authorized until September 30, 2018, in accordance with the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2018
context: Stale for planning: the current expiry date of E-Verify's authorization, which Congress extends in appropriations laws, was not verified and must be checked before January 2029.

statement: The Dallas Fed reported that half of newly hired workers nationwide were vetted through E-Verify in 2015 and that twenty-one states required its use as of December 2016, eight with universal mandates.
anchor: half of newly hired workers nationwide vetted through the system in 2015
Twenty-one states required use of the program as of December 2016
only eight states have universal mandates covering all employers
context: Federal Reserve Bank report (Orrenius and Zavodny). State counts have changed since; 2026 search results suggest more states and new mandates (Ohio construction, Florida bills) but were not verified.

statement: The Dallas Fed found the number of likely unauthorized immigrants and workers fell below expected levels in five states with E-Verify mandates, including Arizona and Georgia.
anchor: the number of unauthorized immigrants and/or unauthorized immigrant workers fell below what would have been expected absent E-Verify in five states—Alabama, Arizona, Georgia, Mississippi and Utah
context: Synthetic-control counterfactual estimates using likely-unauthorized populations from survey data; the effect on employment was larger than on population (their later section).

statement: Bohn, Lofstrom and Raphael found a notable, statistically significant reduction in Arizona's foreign-born and Hispanic noncitizen population share after the Legal Arizona Workers Act.
anchor: We document a notable and statistically significant reduction in the proportion of the Arizona population that is foreign-born and in particular, that is Hispanic noncitizen.
context: Peer-reviewed synthetic-control study of Arizona only; cannot separate E-Verify from other 2007-2010 Arizona enforcement and the recession. They find no similar decline for Hispanic naturalized citizens.

statement: The same authors found that the Arizona mandate did not appear to have improved labor market outcomes of competing legal low-skilled workers.
anchor: the Legal Arizona Workers Act does not appear to have improved labor market outcomes of competing legal low-skilled workers
context: Peer-reviewed; synthetic control on Arizona; abstract also reports some evidence of diminished employment among legal low-skilled workers, concentrated among non-Hispanic white men.

statement: Amuedo-Dorantes and Bansak found that universal and public-sector E-Verify mandates reduced employment of likely unauthorized workers and increased the employment likelihood of native workers.
anchor: We find that the enactment of both universal and public-sector only mandates reduce employment of likely unauthorized workers.
but increases the employment likelihood of native workers
context: Peer-reviewed multi-state difference-in-differences; results differ from the Arizona-only synthetic control in EV-IMM-401, so the native-worker effect is contested.

statement: DHS estimated that 9 million lawful permanent residents were eligible to naturalize as of January 2023, about 71 percent of the 12.7 million living in the United States.
anchor: estimates that as of January 2023, 9 million LPRs were eligible to naturalize, based on meeting age and residency requirements, representing approximately 71% of the 12.7 million LPRs residing in the United States
context: DHS Office of Homeland Security Statistics estimate relayed by CRS in 2025; eligibility is based on age and residency only, not on English, civics or good moral character.

statement: About 818,500 people naturalized in fiscal year 2024, against an average of roughly 758,000 a year over the previous 20 years.
anchor: On average, during the last 20 years, approximately 758,000 individuals naturalized annually
In FY2024, approximately 818,500 persons naturalized.
context: USCIS and DHS Yearbook counts as relayed by CRS.

statement: The naturalization application fee was $760 on paper or $710 online as of September 2025, with reduced fees and waivers for some applicants.
anchor: (currently $760 for paper filing or $710 for online filing). Reduced fees and fee waivers are available to certain applicants.
context: 2024 fee rule (effective April 1, 2024). See EV-IMM-423 for the proposed increase.

statement: In June 2026 DHS proposed raising the N-400 fee from $760 to $1,330 on paper and ending fee waivers and the reduced fee, with military applicants still exempt.
anchor:
DHS proposes to increase the general
paper filing fee for Form N–400 from

$760 to $1,330

to
end both the reduced fee option for
Form N–400, and the availability of fee
waivers for both forms
context: Second Trump administration proposed rule, 91 FR 37500; comments closed 2026-08-24; final status unknown as of 2026-11-12. The online fee would rise from $710 to $1,280.

statement: The 2024 fee rule gave a 50 percent discount, a $380 N-400 fee, to applicants with household incomes between 150 and 400 percent of the poverty guidelines.
anchor:
The rule also introduced a 50% discount for certain low-
income individuals who may not qualify for a fee waiver. Those whose household incomes are
between 150% and 400% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines (FPG) pay a discounted fee of $380.
context: Biden-era rule; the June 2026 proposal would end this reduced fee (EV-IMM-423).

statement: Offering a fee voucher doubled the naturalization application rate among low-income immigrants in a New York experiment, while common nudges did not raise applications among fee-waiver-eligible immigrants below the poverty level.
anchor: offering fee vouchers doubles the naturalization application rate among low-income immigrants, but nudges often used by service providers did not increase applications among fee waiver-eligible immigrants below the poverty level
context: Peer-reviewed randomized experiment in New York (PNAS 2018). Applications, not completed naturalizations; the fee deterrent applies to those who pay the full fee. The PNAS abstract wording was read via the GLOBALCIT page.

statement: The median N-400 processing time was 5.5 months in the first nine months of fiscal year 2025, with about 536,000 applications pending on March 31, 2025.
anchor: The median processing time for the N-400 was 5.5 months in the first nine months of FY2025. As of March 31, 2025, approximately 536,000 naturalization applications were pending
context: USCIS data as relayed by CRS.

statement: In August 2025 USCIS announced it would resume "neighborhood investigations" of naturalization applicants, a departure from policy since 1991.
anchor: In a departure from USCIS policy since 1991, in August 2025, USCIS announced it would exercise its statutory authority to conduct personal investigations of naturalization applicants
context: Second Trump administration policy as described by CRS; effect on approvals or processing times not yet measurable here.

statement: In fiscal year 2023, 823,702 lawful permanent residents applied to naturalize, well below the estimated 9 million eligible.
anchor:
In FY2023, 823,702 LPRs submitted naturalization applications. The number of individuals who have recently applied for
citizenship remains well below the estimated population of 9 million LPRs
context: USCIS counts as relayed by CRS (Biden-era). The 9 million is a DHS estimate of eligibility by age and residency only (EV-IMM-420).

statement: The National Academies committee found that children of immigrants meet or exceed the schooling of typical third-generation and later native-born Americans, though second-generation Mexicans and Central Americans do not reach parity.
anchor: their children meet or exceed the schooling level of typical third-generation and higher native-born Americans.

some immigrant groups, such as Mexicans and Central Americans, have an average education of less than 10 years, and although their children attain an average of over 12 years of education, the second generation does not reach parity with the general native-born population
context: Consensus committee synthesis; the data are from before 2015, and the statement about parity is for groups with low-schooling parents.

statement: The committee reported male employment of 86 percent for first-generation immigrants and 83 percent for the second generation, and female employment of 61 percent for immigrants against 72 percent for the native born.
anchor: the male employment rate for all educational levels is 86 percent; this is higher than the general population of native-born Americans. The second-generation employment rate is slightly lower at 83 percent. Among women, the pattern is reversed with a 61 percent employment rate for immigrants, which is lower than the 72 percent for the native born.
locator: News release, Employment and earnings paragraph
context: Pre-2015 data summarized in the release; current rates differ.

statement: The committee found foreign-born men aged 18 to 39 are incarcerated at one-fourth the rate of native-born men of the same age, with crime rates rising toward the native-born level by the second and third generations.
anchor: Foreign-born men age 18-39 are incarcerated at one-fourth the rate of native-born American men of the same age. However, in the second and third generations, crime rates increase and resemble that of the general population of native-born Americans.
context: Consensus committee synthesis; the same release reports health and family-pattern advantages also declining across generations, so integration is not uniformly positive.

statement: Canada's 2025-2027 levels plan cut permanent resident targets from 500,000 to 395,000 in 2025 and 380,000 in 2026, and set 365,000 for 2027.
anchor: reducing from 500,000 permanent residents to 395,000 in 2025
reducing from 500,000 permanent residents to 380,000 in 2026
setting a target of 365,000 permanent residents in 2027
context: Canadian government plan announced October 2024 and superseded by the 2026-2028 plan (EV-IMM-451). Quotation from a fetch extract; reviewer to confirm wording.

statement: Canada's latest levels plan holds permanent resident targets at 380,000 in each of its three years, with the economic category reaching 64 percent of admissions.
anchor: Targets for permanent residents have been stabilized at 380,000 across all three years
with the economic category reaching 64% of admissions
locator: CIMM briefing note, permanent resident targets
context: Canadian government briefing, December 2025. Quotation from a fetch extract; reviewer to confirm wording. Temporary-resident targets (not verified) were cut further.

anchor: reduce temporary resident volumes to 5% of Canada’s population by the end of 2026
context: A policy goal, not an outcome; attainment was not checked. Quotation from a fetch extract; reviewer to confirm wording.

statement: As of February 2026 Canada's Immigration and Refugee Board had approximately 298K refugee claims pending, with an average wait for a decision of 18 months.

context: Canadian government briefing note. A claim filed in 2026 could wait about three years for a first decision, the note says. Much of the inventory is not ready to be heard (security screening), per a separate March 2026 briefing seen only in search results. Quotation from a fetch extract; reviewer to confirm wording.

statement: Spain's 2026 extraordinary regularisation, open from 16 April to 30 June, drew 1,174,978 applications, 79.6 percent on grounds of strong ties and 20.4 percent from international protection applicants.
anchor: has concluded with a total of 1,174,978 applications registered, of which 609,737 have already been processed.
79.6% relate to authorisations granted on exceptional grounds due to strong ties to the country
the remaining 20.4% relate to authorisations for applicants for international protection.
launched by the Ministry of Inclusion, Social Security and Migration on 16 April and which ended on 30 June
context: Spanish government count; about double the government's forecast of roughly 500,000 per press reports not verified here. 609,737 had been processed at the time of release. Quotation from a fetch extract; reviewer to confirm wording.

statement: Spain's legalization covered around 600,000 working-age immigrants, and payroll-tax revenue rose by 4,189 euros per legalized immigrant at the province level.
anchor: resulted in the legalization of around 600,000 working-age immigrants already working illegally in Spain
legalized immigrant, payroll-tax revenues increased by 4,189 euros at the province level
context: Cross-province difference-in-differences from a 2019 working paper (published later in the Journal of Labor Economics; published numbers not checked). Abstract says "at least 4,000 euros". The same paper finds no magnet effect.

statement: The same study found that the Spanish legalization did not lead to magnet effects, comparing non-EU to EU immigrants.
anchor: legalization of 600,000 non-EU immigrants by the unexpectedly elected Spanish government following the terrorist attacks of 2004
the policy did not lead to magnet effects
context: Working paper abstract; magnet effect means new unauthorized arrivals attracted by the expectation of future legalization. Spain's 2026 round is far larger, so the finding may not carry over.

statement: The EU Asylum Procedure Regulation applies from 12 June 2026 to applications lodged on or after that date.
anchor:
This Regulation shall apply from 12 June 2026.
3. This Regulation shall apply to the procedure for granting international protection in relation to applications lodged as from 12 June 2026.
context: EU primary law (Regulation (EU) 2024/1348). Member-state implementation readiness was reported as uncertain in news items not verified here.

statement: The regulation says the asylum border procedure should in any event not exceed 12 weeks, extendable to 16 weeks where the person is transferred to another Member State.
anchor: It should in any event not exceed 12 weeks, including the determination of the Member State responsible. Member States should be able to extend this deadline to 16 weeks
context: A recital, not an operative article; operative Article 51 sets the same limit but was not separately anchored.

statement: The border procedure applies where the applicant's nationality has an EU-wide recognition share of 20 percent or lower of decisions.
anchor: is, according to the latest available yearly Union-wide average Eurostat data, 20 % or lower
context: The text allows exceptions where the situation in the country has changed significantly or the applicant belongs to a category for whom 20 percent is not representative.

statement: The UK Home Office reported 86,000 asylum claims in the year ending June 2026, 21 percent fewer than the previous year, with a grant rate of 38 percent against 48 percent.

the grant rate in the YE June 2026 was 38%
down from 48% in the previous year

56% fewer than at the end of June 2025
16,000 supported asylum seekers (17%) were in hotel accommodation, 50% lower than a year earlier
context: UK official statistics. The initial-decision backlog fell but the appeals backlog was reported rising (search snippet, unverified). Quotation from a fetch extract; reviewer to confirm wording.

at an estimated cost equal to A$5.6 million (US$3.9 million) per person
context: Advocacy organization citing Australian department estimates; I did not reach the underlying Senate or audit document. Quotation from a fetch extract; reviewer to confirm wording.

context: Presidential determinations as tabulated by CRS. Covers only FY2006-FY2017: the 1980-2005 ceilings were NOT retrieved, so the legacy claim that a 50,000 floor sits below every ceiling from 1980 to 2016 is only checked for 2006-2016 (it holds there, since the lowest was 70,000).

statement: After the terrorist attacks of that period refugee admissions fell to historically low levels, with 27,131 admitted in fiscal year 2002.

plunged to historically low levels in the years following the attacks. In FY2002, for
example, actual admissions totaled 27,131.
context: Actual admissions, not the ceiling, which was higher; admissions below a ceiling do not contradict the ceiling-floor claim. Ceiling for FY2002 was not retrieved.

there
were significantly fewer admissions in FY2011 (56,424) and FY2012 (58,238); the refugee

a smaller share of GARs expressed satisfaction compared to PSRs and BVORs

Quotation from a fetch extract; reviewer to confirm wording.

statement: The Australian Review of the Migration System concluded in March 2023 that Australia's migration program is not fit for purpose and needs major reform rather than tinkering.

Creating a fit for purpose system will require major reform, it cannot be
achieved by further tinkering and incrementalism.
context: Independent three-person expert panel for the Albanese government; findings are the panel's judgement. The government's response was the December 2023 Migration Strategy (not read).

statement: The Australian review counted more than 1.8 million temporary migrants with the legal ability to work in Australia and warned against a permanently temporary underclass.

we now have more than 1.8 million temporary migrants living
in Australia with the legal ability to participate in our labour market

there is clear evidence of systemic exploitation and the risk of an emerging
permanently temporary underclass
context: Count as given by the review panel in March 2023.

statement: The NYIFUP evaluation reported that clients had lived in the United States on average 16 years when deportation proceedings began.
anchor: NYIFUP clients had been living in the United States for 16 years
context: Shows who the program serves (long-resident people with US-citizen children, per the summary).

statement: The 2015 National Academies release said more than 90 percent of Americans polled say it is very or fairly important that people living in the U.S. speak English, and today's immigrants are learning English at the same rate or faster than earlier waves.
anchor: More than 90 percent of Americans polled
today’s immigrants are learning English at the same rate or faster than earlier waves of immigrants
context: Committee synthesis in the news release; the same release says the K-12 system is not equipped for nearly 5 million English-language learners.

statement: The U.S. Citizenship Act would give "lawful prospective immigrant" status valid for 6 years, and holders could adjust to permanent residence after at least 5 years in that status once they have satisfied any applicable federal tax liability.
anchor: (1) shall remain valid for 6 years, unless revoked pursuant to subsection 245G(g)(4); and
(3) has been a lawful prospective immigrant for not less than 5 years;
(6) has satisfied any applicable Federal tax liability.
context: Bill as introduced February 18, 2021 in the 117th Congress by Democrats (Biden administration framework); not enacted and no floor vote was found. This is the 8-year-path model the legacy IMM-1 draws on. Initial grant also needs background checks and fees under proposed INA 245G.

statement: The U.S. Citizenship Act would require continuous physical presence in the United States beginning on January 1, 2021, and would bar those who were lawful permanent residents, refugees or asylees on that date from the new statuses.

(A) In general A noncitizen shall be ineligible for status under sections 245B, 245C, 245D, 245E, and 245F if on January 1, 2021, the noncitizen was any of the following:

statement: The U.S. Citizenship Act would let agricultural workers who performed agricultural labor or services for at least 2,300 hours or 400 work days in the preceding 5 years apply directly for lawful permanent resident status.
anchor: (3) the Secretary determines that, during the 5-year period immediately preceding the date on which the noncitizen submits an application under this section, the noncitizen performed agricultural labor or services for at least 2,300 hours or 400 work days.
context: Proposed INA 245F. Compare the Farm Workforce Modernization Act (EV-IMM-522), which uses a different work test and a longer path.

anchor: (3) subject to section 245G(b)(3)(B)(ii), has been continuously physically present in the United States since January 1, 2017; and
(B) was eligible for deferred enforced departure as of January 1, 2017.
context: Proposed INA 245E. The 2017 date fixes the covered countries; Haitian and Syrian TPS holders whose status ended in 2026 (per the legacy file) would depend on the date and designation test.

statement: The U.S. Citizenship Act would let people who entered the United States before age 18 and who meet a diploma plus degree, military service or work test apply directly for lawful permanent resident status, with a streamlined procedure for people granted DACA.
anchor: (3) was younger than 18 years of age on the date on which the noncitizen initially entered the United States;

context: Proposed INA 245D, the Dream Act title of the bill. The work route requires earned income for periods totaling not less than 3 years (same section).

statement: The U.S. Citizenship Act would set the processing fee at a level sufficient to recover the cost of processing the application and would let the Secretary cap the fee for a family or waive it for good cause; it sets no dollar penalty in the text of the new statuses.
anchor: (B) Recovery of costs The processing fee referred to in subparagraph (A) shall be set at a level sufficient to recover the cost of processing the application.
(ii) for good cause, exempt individual applicants or defined classes of applicants from the requirement to pay fees under this paragraph.
context: Contrast S. 744 (a $1,000 penalty, EV-IMM-525) and the Dignity Act (restitution, EV-IMM-510 and 511). The legacy IMM-1 design follows this cost-recovery model.

statement: The U.S. Citizenship Act would allow a lawful permanent resident who was lawfully present and eligible for employment authorization for not less than 3 years before becoming a permanent resident to be naturalized without waiting the usual period.
anchor: (f) Notwithstanding section 316(a)(1), any lawful permanent resident who was lawfully present in the United States and eligible for employment authorization for not less than 3 years before becoming a lawful permanent resident may be naturalized upon compliance with all other requirements under this chapter.
context: Amends INA 318 and is the citizenship shortcut that makes the bill an "8-year path" (about 5 years in provisional status, then permanent residence and naturalization). The exact total depends on how the 3 years are counted; a reviewer should confirm by reading the whole section.

statement: The 2025 Dignity Act would require an applicant for the Dignity Program to prove continuous physical presence since December 31, 2020 and to include a restitution payment of at least $1,000.
anchor: (A) That the alien has been continually physically present in the United States since December 31, 2020.
