context: Introduced July 15, 2025 by Rep. Salazar (R-FL) and Rep. Escobar (D-TX) in the 119th Congress; no committee action found. The cutoff moved from "at least 5 years prior to enactment" in the 2023 version (EV-IMM-516) to a fixed date.

statement: The 2025 Dignity Act would defer action for 7 years and require participants to pay an additional fee of at least $1,000 with each biennial report until a total of $7,000 has been paid, with an exception for people who held temporary protected status before the Act.
anchor: shall issue an order deferring further action for a period of 7 years.
shall pay an additional fee of at least $1,000 with each report under paragraph (1), until a total of $7,000 has been paid
Subparagraph (A) shall not apply to any individual who had temporary protected status under section 244 of the Immigration and Nationality Act
context: The restitution money goes to the H-1B Nonimmigrant Petitioner Account for American-worker programs (title IV of the division). Other conditions in the same section include a 1 percent levy on adjusted gross income (EV-IMM-513) and payment of assessed federal income tax liability within 7 years.

statement: Dignity status under the 2025 Dignity Act is valid for 7 years, may be renewed any number of times, and gives lawful status as a nonimmigrant plus work authorization; the Dignity Program section itself contains no adjustment to permanent residence except through military enlistment.
anchor: (1) shall be valid for a period of 7 years;
(2) may be renewed any number of times; and
(A) lawful status as a nonimmigrant;
that individual shall be eligible to adjust to lawful permanent resident status through the Armed Forces.
context: This is why the legacy file and press describe the bill as status without a citizenship path. People in the bill's separate Dream Act title (EV-IMM-515) and other categories can still reach permanent residence. The 2023 version had a Redemption Program with a permanent-residence route (EV-IMM-517); the saved 2025 text has no Redemption section (searched, zero hits for the word).

statement: Dignity Program participants under the 2025 Dignity Act may not use any federal means-tested benefits or entitlement programs and owe a tax of 1 percent of adjusted gross income on employment income, deposited in the Immigration Infrastructure and Debt Reduction Fund.
anchor: the participant shall not avail himself or herself of any Federal means-tested benefits or entitlement programs.
a tax equal to 1 percent of the adjusted gross income
Any tax collected under this paragraph shall be deposited in the Immigration Infrastructure and Debt Reduction Fund
context: A benefit bar that applies for the whole program; benefits received by a U.S.-citizen child in the same household are carved out (same paragraph). Tied to the shared eligibility table in dossiers/shared-rules.md.

statement: The 2025 Dignity Act would require anyone present without lawful status, and not in its other programs, to apply for the Dignity Program or depart the United States within 12 months of enactment.
anchor: (b) Departure Not later than 12 months after the date of the enactment of this Act, any alien present in the United States without lawful status under the immigration laws, or not participating in the programs outlined in division B under this Act shall apply for the Dignity Program or depart the United States.
context: The 12-month window pairs with the bill's mandatory E-Verify (EV-IMM-515). The bill also offers "intentional self-deportation" without the 3- and 10-year reentry bars for those who leave within 12 months.

(1) valid for a period of 10 years, unless such period is extended by the Secretary; and

statement: The 2023 Dignity Act required applicants for the Dignity Program to have been continually physically present at least 5 years before enactment and to pay a restitution of at least $1,000 up front and a total of $5,000.

statement: ICE reported 483,200 deportations in FY26, a record, against 442,640 in FY25.
anchor: In FY26, ICE carried out 483,200 deportations, which broke the record for the highest number of deportations in the agency's history.
This surpasses the previous record held by FY25, which saw 442,640 deportations.
context: ICE press release of November 12, 2026, issued by the agency that carries out removals under the second Trump administration; the agency has a stake in reporting a high count. The release gives no definition or table. ICE's statistics page defines its removal data as including returns (voluntary returns, voluntary departures and withdrawals under docket control), so the two counts may include them; the release itself does not say. The FY2025 count is the release's figure, not from an ICE annual report: as of mid-March 2026 the FY2025 annual report had not been published (AP, March 15, 2026, not saved). Compare ICE's FY2024 count of 271,484 removals of people with final orders (ICE Annual Report FY2024, not saved), which uses a different definition.
